specPoints.text: determine acceleration from the gradient of a velocity−time graph

primer.text: The distance-time graph answered 'how far by when'; the velocity-time graph answers the sharper question of how the pace itself evolved. This lesson teaches the graph's vocabulary of slopes and flats, then extracts a number from the picture by measuring its gradient.

lessons.title: Reading slopes and flats on a velocity-time graph
lessons.opening: On this graph the story is told entirely by the line's direction and steepness: rising means gaining speed, falling means losing it, and a flat stretch means cruising unchanged. This lesson builds the full reading vocabulary before any numbers are taken from the plot.
keyPoints: A velocity-time graph plots the object's velocity against time, so the vertical axis carries m/s and the horizontal axis carries seconds.
A straight sloping line means the acceleration is constant for that whole stretch.
The steepness of the slope carries the size of the acceleration: steep means fast-changing, gentle means gradual.
A positive gradient shows the velocity increasing; a negative gradient shows it decreasing.
A flat horizontal line means zero acceleration, which is motion at a steady velocity.

low.restatement: Look at which way the line tilts: up means the object gains speed, down means it loses speed, and level means the speed holds steady. How steep the tilt is tells you how quickly the speed changes.
low.analogy: Picture a hiking trail map where height is the speed: climbing stretches gain speed, descending stretches lose it, and the flat plateaus cruise.
low.examPointer: Describe sections with the motion word first (accelerating, decelerating, constant velocity), then justify it from the slope's tilt.

medium.restatement: Because the vertical axis is velocity, the gradient of the line is the acceleration. A single straight section therefore has one constant acceleration across it, and only a bend between sections changes the acceleration's value.
medium.analogy: The line behaves like a car's accelerator pedal held at one setting: the slope is the pedal pressure, and a new section is a new pedal setting.
medium.examPointer: Two-line comparison questions are decided by steepness alone: the steeper line carries the larger acceleration even if it sits lower on the graph.

check.stem: On a velocity-time graph, what does a flat horizontal section of the line show?

options.text: Zero acceleration, so the velocity holds a steady value
options.explanation: No tilt means no change of velocity per second: cruising at one constant velocity.

options.text: The object has stopped moving altogether
options.explanation: Stopped would mean the velocity line sits ON the time axis at zero, not merely flat above it.

options.text: The acceleration is at its largest
options.explanation: Largest acceleration belongs to the steepest slope; a flat line has no slope at all.

options.text: The object is decelerating gently
options.explanation: Deceleration needs a downward tilt; a level line has none.

check.stem: Two straight sections appear on a velocity-time graph: one shallow, one steep, both rising. What do they share and how do they differ?

options.text: Both show constant acceleration; the steeper one has the larger acceleration
options.explanation: Any straight section is constant acceleration, and steepness ranks the acceleration's size.

options.text: Both show the same acceleration because both rise
options.explanation: Rising fixes the sign, not the size; steepness sets how large the acceleration is.

options.text: The shallow one shows deceleration because it changes slowly
options.explanation: A gentle rise is a small positive acceleration, not a negative one.

options.text: Neither shows constant acceleration unless the line is flat
options.explanation: Constancy of acceleration is exactly what a straight section means.

check.stem: A line on a velocity-time graph tilts steadily downward. What is happening to the object?

options.text: Its velocity is decreasing, so it is decelerating
options.explanation: A negative gradient reads directly as decreasing velocity.

options.text: It is moving backwards along its path
options.explanation: Backwards travel would need the velocity itself to go negative, which a downward tilt alone does not show.

options.text: It is accelerating, because all motion counts as acceleration
options.explanation: Losing speed is deceleration; the sign of the gradient settles which.

options.text: Its velocity is unchanged; only its distance changes
options.explanation: On this graph the vertical axis IS the velocity, so a tilt is a velocity change.

check.stem: Which quantity belongs on the vertical axis of a velocity-time graph?

options.text: Velocity, in metres per second
options.explanation: The graph is named for its axes: velocity up, time along.

options.text: Distance travelled, in metres
options.explanation: Distance on the vertical axis makes it a distance-time graph, the sibling graph from earlier in this section.

options.text: Acceleration, in m/s²
options.explanation: Acceleration is read FROM the gradient here; it is not the plotted quantity.

options.text: Time, in seconds
options.explanation: Time always runs along the horizontal axis on these motion graphs.

check.stem: A graph shows a straight rising section followed by a flat section. How should the two sections be described?

options.text: Constant acceleration first, then constant velocity
options.explanation: The rising straight is steady acceleration; the flat continuation is steady velocity.

options.text: Increasing acceleration first, then acceleration
options.explanation: A straight rise has one fixed acceleration; only a curve steepens.

options.text: Constant velocity first, then deceleration
options.explanation: That reverses both sections; the flat stretch comes second in this graph.

options.text: Deceleration first, then rest
options.explanation: A rising tilt and a flat line above the axis are neither deceleration nor rest.

check.stem: State what a straight sloping line on a velocity-time graph tells you about the acceleration.
check.modelAnswer: A straight sloping line means the acceleration is constant: the velocity changes by the same amount every second along that section.

check.stem: Recall what the steepness of the slope on a velocity-time graph represents.
check.modelAnswer: The steepness (slope) represents the magnitude of the acceleration: a steep slope is a large acceleration and a gentle slope is a small one.

check.stem: Explain why a flat line and a line sitting on the time axis describe two different physical situations on a velocity-time graph.
check.modelAnswer: A flat line above the axis fixes the velocity at some non-zero steady value: the object cruises. A line lying on the time axis fixes the velocity at zero: the object is at rest. The height of the flat stretch is the velocity itself, so height, not flatness, separates cruising from stopping.

check.stem: A velocity-time graph shows an object held at 15 m/s for 8 s, then rising in a straight line to 25 m/s over the next 10 s. Describe both sections and state which section has the larger acceleration.
check.modelAnswer: The first section is constant velocity (zero acceleration) at 15 m/s for 8 s; the second is a straight rise, a constant acceleration of (25 − 15) / 10 = 1.0 m/s². The second section has the larger acceleration, since the first has none.

lessons.title: Acceleration from the gradient
sourceHeadings: How to find acceleration on a velocity-time graph
lessons.opening: The picture now becomes a calculator. Because the vertical axis is velocity, the gradient of any straight section is numerically the acceleration, and a large, clearly-drawn gradient triangle turns the reading into a mark-earning calculation. This lesson drills that extraction on the cyclist's training graph.
keyPoints: The acceleration equals the gradient of the velocity-time line: acceleration = gradient = Δy / Δx.
Δy is the change in velocity read off the vertical axis; Δx is the matching change in time from the horizontal axis.
Draw the gradient triangle as large as the section allows, and take both changes straight from the axis scales with their units.
The worked reading for the cyclist between 5 s and 10 s: Δv = 5 m/s over Δt = 5 s, giving a = 1 m/s².

low.restatement: Pick the straight section, draw a big right-triangle under it, then divide how much the velocity rose by how long the rise took. That quotient is the acceleration.
low.analogy: It is exactly like reading a road's steepness sign: rise over run, except the rise is a speed and the run is a time.
low.examPointer: Examiners award credit for a large gradient triangle drawn ON the graph; a tiny triangle squeezed between gridlines invites reading error.

medium.restatement: Gradient extraction is the graphical twin of a = Δv/t: Δy plays Δv, Δx plays t. The section's straightness is what makes one number describe the whole interval.
medium.analogy: A single gradient number summarises the section the way one average summarises a whole trip: lawful precisely because the line is straight.
medium.examPointer: State the unit with the answer: a gradient read as (5 m/s)/(5 s) is 1 m/s², never a bare 1.

check.stem: Which reading must be taken from the vertical axis when extracting acceleration from a velocity-time gradient?

options.text: The change in velocity across the chosen section
options.explanation: Δy is the velocity change; it is the numerator of the gradient and of a = Δv/t.

options.text: The velocity at the start of the whole graph
options.explanation: The starting velocity of the graph is irrelevant; only the change across the section enters.

options.text: The highest velocity anywhere on the plot
options.explanation: A peak value is not the section's change; the triangle fixes which two heights matter.

options.text: The area beneath the line
options.explanation: Area belongs to the distance reading of the next lesson, not to the gradient.

check.stem: A straight section carries the velocity from 8 m/s up to 20 m/s across 6 s. What acceleration does the gradient give?

options.explanation: Δv = 12 m/s over Δt = 6 s gives a gradient of 2.0 m/s².

options.text: 3.3 m/s², from 20 ÷ 6
options.explanation: Dividing the final velocity by the time ignores the 8 m/s the object already had.

options.text: 0.50 m/s², from 6 ÷ 12
options.explanation: That inverts the quotient; the velocity change divides by the time.

options.text: 12 m/s², quoting the velocity change as the rate
options.explanation: 12 m/s is Δv; the division by 6 s is what makes it a rate.

check.stem: Why do examiners prefer a large gradient triangle drawn on the graph?

options.text: A larger triangle spreads the readings across more gridlines, so each read value is more reliable
options.explanation: Bigger rises and runs mean the same half-square-line reading error is a smaller fraction of each value.

options.text: Large triangles make the gradient come out positive
options.explanation: The sign comes from the tilt, not the triangle's size.

options.text: Small triangles are banned by the mark scheme
options.explanation: Nothing is banned; small triangles just lose precision and credit for the drawn construction.

options.text: A large triangle removes the need to state units
options.explanation: Units are always required on the final acceleration, whatever the triangle's size.

check.stem: On the cyclist's training graph, the section between 5 s and 10 s rises by 5 m/s. What acceleration does that section carry?

options.text: 1 m/s², from 5 m/s over 5 s
options.explanation: Δv = 5 m/s and Δt = 10 − 5 = 5 s, so a = 5/5 = 1 m/s².

options.text: 5 m/s², from 5 ÷ 1
options.explanation: The 5 in the denominator must be the 5-second interval, not a bare 1.

options.text: 0.5 m/s², from 5 ÷ 10
options.explanation: Dividing by the absolute timestamp 10 s forgets that the section starts at 5 s.

options.text: 2 m/s², from 10 ÷ 5
options.explanation: That divides the timestamps rather than the changes; the quotient must be Δv over Δt.

check.stem: A gradient triangle is drawn on a downward-sloping section. The velocity falls 6 m/s across 3 s. What should be concluded?

options.text: The gradient is −2 m/s²: a deceleration of 2 m/s²
options.explanation: The fall of 6 m/s across 3 s gives a signed gradient of −2 m/s², read as decelerating at 2 m/s².

options.text: The gradient is +2 m/s² because the triangle is drawn upward
options.explanation: The construction is drawn for measurement; the sign comes from the falling velocity.

options.text: The gradient is −18 m/s², multiplying 6 by 3
options.explanation: Gradient divides the changes; multiplication has no place in the reading.

options.text: No acceleration can be found from a falling line
options.explanation: Falling lines carry perfectly good negative gradients; the method is unchanged.

check.stem: State the relationship between a velocity-time gradient and acceleration in symbols.
check.modelAnswer: Acceleration = gradient = Δy / Δx, where Δy is the change in velocity and Δx is the change in time across the straight section.

check.stem: Recall the two practical instructions for drawing a gradient triangle on an exam graph.
check.modelAnswer: Draw it as large as the section allows, and take both the velocity change and the time change directly from the axis scales with their units.

check.stem: Explain why one single gradient value can describe a whole straight section of a velocity-time graph.
check.modelAnswer: Along a straight line the gradient is the same at every point, and on this graph that gradient IS the acceleration. A straight section therefore has one unchanging acceleration, so one triangle anywhere on the section returns the value that holds for the entire interval.

check.stem: A tram's velocity falls from 18 m/s to 6 m/s in a straight section lasting 4.0 s. Use the gradient to calculate the acceleration and state the motion word for it.
check.modelAnswer: Δv = 6 − 18 = −12 m/s over Δt = 4.0 s, so the gradient is −3.0 m/s²; the negative value is a deceleration.

glossary.definition: A plot of velocity (vertical, m/s) against time (horizontal, s) for a moving object.
Motion with unchanging velocity, shown by a flat horizontal line and meaning zero acceleration.
The steepness of a line, Δy/Δx; on a velocity-time graph it equals the acceleration.
A large right-triangle drawn on a straight section so its rise and run can be read from the axis scales.

workedExample.prompt: A cyclist trains along a flat, straight road. The velocity-time graph shows five sections A to E. (a) In which section is the cyclist's acceleration the largest? (b) Calculate the cyclist's acceleration between 5 and 10 seconds.
steps: Recall that the slope of a velocity-time graph gives the magnitude of the acceleration, so only the sloping sections (B and D) are accelerating; A, C and E are flat, i.e. constant velocity.
Compare the slopes of B and D: section D is the steeper of the two, so the largest acceleration is in section D.
For the 5 s to 10 s interval, draw a large gradient triangle and read the changes from the axes: Δv = 5 m/s and Δt = 5 s.
workedExample.finalAnswer: (a) section D; (b) a = 1 m/s² between 5 s and 10 s
